**Summary of the Report on Legislative Branch Agency Appointments**

The report provides an overview of the appointment processes for the leaders of eight key legislative branch agencies and entities, including the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the Library of Congress, the Government Publishing Office (GPO), the Office of the Architect of the Capitol, the U.S. Capitol Police, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the Congressional Research Service (CRS), and the Office of Compliance. These appointments are governed by a mix of presidential, congressional, and independent procedures, reflecting a complex and evolving system of oversight and accountability.

The first four agencies—GAO, the Library of Congress, GPO, and the Office of the Architect of the Capitol—are led by individuals appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. The CBO director is appointed entirely by Congress, while the CRS director is selected by the Librarian of Congress. The Office of Compliance is led by an executive director appointed by the board of directors, and the Register of Copyrights is currently appointed by the Librarian of Congress.

The report highlights the historical development and ongoing debates surrounding the appointment processes. For instance, the Architect of the Capitol was previously appointed by the President for an unlimited term, but the 1990 Legislative Branch Appropriations Act established a 10-year term and a congressional commission to recommend candidates. Several bills in the 111th and 115th Congresses sought to shift the appointment authority from the President to congressional leaders, but none were enacted. These proposals reflect broader concerns about the balance of power, the role of Congress in the appointment process, and the interpretation of the Appointments Clause of the Constitution.

The report also details the tenure, reappointment, and removal provisions for each agency head, as well as their salaries and benefits. For example, the Comptroller General of GAO is appointed for a 15-year term and may be removed only for cause, while the CBO director serves a four-year term and can be removed by either chamber of Congress. The GPO Director has no set term, and the Librarian of Congress, following the 2015 Succession Modernization Act, now serves a maximum of 10 years with the possibility of reappointment.

The report underscores the importance of these appointment mechanisms in ensuring accountability, transparency, and the proper functioning of the legislative branch.
